To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
evoked responses are a combination of dynamic and structural effects and that induced power is a special case of evoked power, where the dynamic effects cancel out.

(a) evoked responses reflect both dynamic (input-dependent) and structural (input-independent) mechanisms; (b) the dynamic mechanisms can be expressed in induced power, and (c) the structural mechanisms can be expressed as a difference between adjusted power and induced power.

(1) induced and evoked power are not necessarily different, (2) induced and evocked power can be different, (3) induced and evokked power can be different and evoked power can be induced, (4) induced power can be adjusted for dynamic effects to obtain structural information.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms generating neuronal responses.
the mechanisms of evoked and oscillatory activity in MEG and EEG,
the mechanisms underlying neuronal transients, and how they are reflected in the evoked and induced components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
evoked and induced oscillations are the results of both dynamic and structural effects.
induced and evoked responses can be attributed to different neuronal mechanisms, but the same neuronal mechanisms can generate both evoked and induced oscillations.
induced and evoked responses are different manifestations of the same neuronal processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
evoked responses are a mixture of structural and dynamic effects.
the relationship between evoked, induced and on-going oscillation is more subtle and nuanced than commonly thought.
the distinction between induced and evoked responses may be more apparent than real.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between evoked and induced oscillations is less clear than previously thought.

, when studying the relationship between neuronal mechanisms and MEG/EEGs responses, it is essential to distinguish between the mechanisms that generate neuronal transients and the mechanisms that generate induced power.
the mechanisms of induced and evoked responses are more closely related than commonly believed.
